Bezalel and Oholiab receive gifts for the work (verses 1–11)

The Israelites had worked as builders and brickmakers in Egypt.

They had not learned the skill needed to produce the intricate workmanship required for the tabernacle.

But the same Holy Spirit who later enabled the apostles to speak in many languages miraculously gave Bezalel and Oholiab the abilities they lacked.

Honor received from God always comes with work to do.

To be employed in his service is itself a great honor.

When God calls people to a task, he either finds them fitted for it or makes them fit for it.

The Lord gives different gifts to different people.

We should each give diligent attention to the particular work entrusted to us.

And whatever skill or wisdom we possess, we must remember that God has put it into our hearts so that we may obey his commands.

The Sabbath must still be observed (verses 12–17)

God had ordered a tabernacle to be built for his worship.

But the people were not to imagine that the sacredness of the work, or their need to finish it quickly, gave them permission to build on the Sabbath.

The Hebrew word shabbath means rest or ceasing from work.

The Sabbath points toward the rest in glory that remains for God's people.

For this reason, Henry argues, the Sabbath's moral obligation continues until time itself gives way to eternity.

Moses receives the stone tablets (verse 18)

God wrote his law on tablets of stone.

Their material showed how enduring the law is.

But it also illustrated the hardness of the human heart.

It would be easier to carve words into stone than to write anything truly good upon our naturally corrupt hearts.

The tablets were written by the finger of God—by his will and power.

Only God can write his law on the human heart.

He gives us hearts of flesh.

Then, through his Spirit, who is called the finger of God, he writes his will within us (2 Corinthians 3:3).

[Exod.31.1-Exod.31.11]
Chapter 31
Chapter Outline
Bezaleel and Aholiab are appointed and qualified for the work of the tabernacle. | (1-11) |
The observance of the sabbath. | (12-17) |
Moses receives the tables of the law. | (18) |
Verses 1-11
The Israelites, who had been masons and bricklayers in Egypt, were not qualified for curious workmanship; but the Spirit who gave the apostles utterance in divers tongues, miraculously gave Bezaleel and Aholiab the skill that was wanting. The honour which comes from God, is always attended with a work to be done; to be employed for God is high honour. Those whom God calls to any service, he will find or make fit for it. The Lord gives different gifts to different persons; let each mind his proper work, diligently remembering that whatever wisdom any one possesses, the Lord put it in the heart, to do his commandments.
[Exod.31.12-Exod.31.17]
Verses 12-17
Orders were now given that a tabernacle should be set up for the service of God. But they must not think that the nature of the work, and the haste that was required, would justify them in working at it on sabbath days. The Hebrew word /shabath/ signifies rest, or ceasing from labour. The thing signified by the sabbath is that rest in glory which remains for the people of God; therefore the moral obligation of the sabbath must continue, till time is swallowed up in eternity.
[Exod.31.18]
Verse 18
The law was written in tables of stone, to show how lasting it is: to denote likewise the hardness of our hearts; one might more easily write on stone, than write any thing good on our corrupt natural hearts. It was written with the finger of God; by his will and power. God only can write his law in the heart: he gives a heart of flesh; then, by his Spirit, which is the finger of God, writes his will in the heart, [2Cor.3.3] 2Co 3:3.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe people cause Aaron to make a golden calf.1–6God's displeasure, The intercession of Moses.7–14Moses breaks the tables of the law, He destroys the golden calf.15–20Aaron's excuse, The idolaters slain.21–29Moses prays for the people.30–35
Israel makes the golden calf (verses 1–6)

While Moses was on the mountain receiving God's law, the people gathered noisily around Aaron.

They had grown tired of waiting for Moses to return.

Impatience leaves people exposed to many temptations.

We must wait for the Lord until he comes, even when he seems to delay.

The people readily gave up their earrings to make an idol.

Their willingness should shame our reluctance to give generously in the service of the true God.

They did not complain about the cost of idolatry.

Why, then, should we begrudge what true religion requires?

Aaron made an image of an ox or calf, shaping it with an engraving tool.

Then the people offered sacrifices to it.

They had put an image before themselves and exchanged God's truth for a lie.

Their sacrifices therefore became detestable.

Only a few days earlier, in that very place, they had heard God command them not to make a carved image.

They had also solemnly promised to obey everything he had said (Exodus 24:7).

Yet they broke his explicit command and defied his clear warning before even leaving the place where they had made the covenant.

This shows that the law has no more power to make us holy than to justify us.

Through it we learn what sin is, but we do not receive sin's cure.

God had appointed Aaron to the priesthood.

Yet a man who had disgraced himself by making an altar for a golden calf could never claim to deserve the honor of serving at God's altar.

He had to acknowledge that he owed it entirely to free grace.

This leaves no room for pride or boasting.

God's anger and Moses' intercession (verses 7–14)

God told Moses that the Israelites had corrupted themselves.

Sin corrupts the sinner, and people corrupt themselves by yielding to their own sinful desires.

They had left the right path.

That is what sin does: it turns us away from duty into a wrong way.

They had quickly forgotten God's mighty works.

God sees what human beings cannot detect.

No evil in the world is hidden from him.

We could not bear to witness even a thousandth part of the wickedness God sees every day.

God revealed the greatness of his just displeasure in a way that human beings could understand.

Moses prayed for the people's deliverance from ruin.

In this, he pictured Christ, through whose mediation alone God reconciles the world to himself.

Moses appealed to God's glory.

Just as honoring God's name ought to be our first request—as it is in the Lord's Prayer—it should also be our principal argument when we pray.

God's promises should likewise be the basis of our prayers.

He is fully able to do everything he has promised.

See how powerful prayer can be!

In response to Moses, God showed his purpose to spare the people, although earlier he had appeared determined to destroy them.

Scripture calls this change in the outward disclosure of God's purpose his relenting from the threatened judgment.

Moses destroys the idol (verses 15–20)

What a sharp contrast Moses experienced!

He came down from a mountain where he had enjoyed fellowship with God and entered a world full of wickedness.

In God's presence he had seen only purity and what is pleasing to him.

Among the people he now found sin and conduct that provoked the Lord.

To show that the idol was nothing at all, Moses ground the golden calf into dust.

He mixed the powder with the people's drink.

This pictured the truth that those who turn away in heart will be made to taste the bitter consequences of their own ways.

Aaron's excuse and the judgment on idolaters (verses 21–29)

No wise person ever offered a more foolish and worthless excuse than Aaron did.

We should never allow other people's words or actions to draw us into sin.

Others can tempt us, but they cannot force us to sin.

When Moses approached, the people's dancing turned to trembling.

Their sin had exposed them to shame.

Moses did not try to remove that disgrace by concealing what had happened or offering a misleading explanation.

He dealt with it by punishing the wrongdoing.

The Levites were commanded to kill the leaders of this rebellion.

Henry says that those executed were the people who openly persisted in standing against God.

Those who persist in sin are heading toward destruction.

In the morning some of these people had been shouting and dancing.

Before night they were dead.

How quickly God's judgments can overturn the careless pleasure of people secure in their sins.

Moses prays again for the people (verses 30–35)

Moses called Israel's wrongdoing a great sin.

One task of ministers is to show people the seriousness of their sins.

The dreadful evil of sin is seen in the great price required for pardon.

Moses pleaded with God for mercy.

He did not come to invent excuses for the people; he came to seek atonement.

We should not understand Moses to mean that he would willingly suffer eternal destruction in the people's place.

We must love our neighbors as ourselves, not more than ourselves.

But with the mind of Christ, Moses was willing to lay down his earthly life, however painfully, if it could preserve his people.

Even Moses could not completely turn aside God's anger.

That showed that the law given through Moses could not reconcile sinners to God or give them perfect peace with him.

Only in Christ does God forgive sin so completely that he remembers it no more.

This history also shows that a proud and worldly heart cannot long endure God's holy commands, humbling truths and spiritual worship.

But a god, a priest, a form of worship, a doctrine and a sacrifice adapted to worldly desires will always find plenty of followers.

Even the gospel itself can be distorted to suit worldly tastes.

How good it is for us that the Prophet greater than Moses, incomparably stronger and more merciful, has made atonement for our souls and continues to intercede for us.

Let us rejoice in his grace!
classic_reading:
[Exod.32.1-Exod.32.6]
Chapter 32
Chapter Outline
The people cause Aaron to make a golden calf. | (1-6) |
God's displeasure, The intercession of Moses. | (7-14) |
Moses breaks the tables of the law, He destroys the golden calf. | (15-20) |
Aaron's excuse, The idolaters slain. | (21-29) |
Moses prays for the people. | (30-35) |
Verses 1-6
While Moses was in the mount, receiving the law from God, the people made a tumultuous address to Aaron. This giddy multitude were weary of waiting for the return of Moses. Weariness in waiting betrays to many temptations. The Lord must be waited for till he comes, and waited for though he tarry. Let their readiness to part with their ear-rings to make an idol, shame our niggardliness in the service of the true God. They did not draw back on account of the cost of their idolatry; and shall we grudge the expenses of religion? Aaron produced the shape of an ox or calf, giving it some finish with a graving tool. They offered sacrifice to this idol. Having set up an image before them, and so changed the truth of God into a lie, their sacrifices were abomination. Had they not, only a few days before, in this very place, heard the voice of the Lord God speaking to them out of the midst of the fire, Thou shalt not make to thyself any graven image? Had they not themselves solemnly entered into covenant with God, that they would do all he had said to them, and would be obedient? ch. 24:7. Yet before they stirred from the place where this covenant had been solemnly made, they brake an express command, in defiance of an express threatening. It plainly shows, that the law was no more able to make holy, than it was to justify; by it is the knowledge of sin, but not the cure of sin. Aaron was set apart by the Divine appointment to the office of the priesthood; but he, who had once shamed himself so far as to build an altar to a golden calf, must own himself unworthy of the honour of attending at the altar of God, and indebted to free grace alone for it. Thus pride and boasting were silenced.
[Exod.32.7-Exod.32.14]
Verses 7-14
God says to Moses, that the Israelites had corrupted themselves. Sin is the corruption of the sinner, and it is a self-corruption; every man is tempted when he is drawn aside of his own lust. They had turned aside out of the way. Sin is a departing from the way of duty into a by-path. They soon forgot God's works. He sees what they cannot discover, nor is any wickedness of the world hid from him. We could not bear to see the thousandth part of that evil which God sees every day. God expresses the greatness of his just displeasure, after the manner of men who would have prayer of Moses could save them from ruin; thus he was a type of Christ, by whose mediation alone, God would reconcile the world to himself. Moses pleads God's glory. The glorifying God's name, as it ought to be our first petition, and it is so in the Lord's prayer, so it ought to be our great plea. And God's promises are to be our pleas in prayer; for what he has promised he is able to perform. See the power of prayer. In answer to the prayers of Moses, God showed his purpose of sparing the people, as he had before seemed determined on their destruction; which change of the outward discovery of his purpose, is called repenting of the evil.
[Exod.32.15-Exod.32.20]
Verses 15-20
What a change it is, to come down from the mount of communion with God, to converse with a wicked world. In God we see nothing but what is pure and pleasing; in the world nothing but what is sinful and provoking. That it might appear an idol is nothing in the world, Moses ground the calf to dust. Mixing this powder with their drink, signified that the backslider in heart should be filled with his own ways.
[Exod.32.21-Exod.32.29]
Verses 21-29
Never did any wise man make a more frivolous and foolish excuse than that of Aaron. We must never be drawn into sin by any thing man can say or do to us; for men can but tempt us to sin, they cannot force us. The approach of Moses turned the dancing into trembling. They were exposed to shame by their sin. The course Moses took to roll away this reproach, was, not by concealing the sin, or putting any false colour upon it, but by punishing it. The Levites were to slay the ringleaders in this wickedness; yet none were executed but those who openly stood forth. Those are marked for ruin who persist in sin: those who in the morning were shouting and dancing, before night were dying. Such sudden changes do the judgments of the Lord sometimes make with sinners that are secure and jovial in their sin.
[Exod.32.30-Exod.32.35]
Verses 30-35
Moses calls it a great sin. The work of ministers is to show people the greatness of their sins. The great evil of sin appears in the price of pardon. Moses pleads with God for mercy; he came not to make excuses, but to make atonement. We are not to suppose that Moses means that he would be willing to perish for ever, for the people's sake. We are to love our neighbour as ourselves, and not more than ourselves. But having that mind which was in Christ, he was willing to lay down his life in the most painful manner, if he might thereby preserve the people. Moses could not wholly turn away the wrath of God; which shows that the law of Moses was not able to reconcile men to God, and to perfect our peace with him. In Christ alone, God so pardons sin as to remember it no more. From this history we see, that no unhumbled, carnal heart, can long endure the holy precepts, the humbling truths, and the spiritual worship of God. But a god, a priest, a worship, a doctrine, and a sacrifice, suited to the carnal mind, will ever meet with abundance of worshippers. The very gospel itself may be so perverted as to suit a worldly taste. Well is it for us, that the Prophet like unto Moses, but who is beyond compare more powerful and merciful, has made atonement for our souls, and now intercedes in our behalf. Let us rejoice in his grace.

God withdraws the assurance of his presence (verses 1–6)

Even when God forgives his people, he must teach them what their sin deserved.

His command to go forward as they were expressed his displeasure powerfully.

He promised to keep his covenant with Abraham by giving the people Canaan.

Yet he withheld the signs of his presence with which he had previously blessed them.

The Israelites mourned over their sin.

Of all sin's painful results, the one true penitents fear and grieve most is the departure of God's presence.

Canaan itself would not be a pleasant land without the Lord.

Those who had gladly surrendered their ornaments to support idolatry could surely lay aside ornaments as a sign of grief and shame for it.

Moses pitches the tent outside the camp (verses 7–11)

Moses took the tabernacle and pitched it outside the camp.

This appears to have been a temporary building used for worship and for hearing disputes among the people.

The Israelites watched Moses as he went to it.

They longed to be restored to peace with God and were deeply concerned about what would happen next.

The pillar of cloud had withdrawn from the camp when the people defiled it through idolatry.

Now it returned.

If our hearts go out to meet God, he will graciously come to meet us.

Moses asks for God's presence and glory (verses 12–23)

Moses pleaded earnestly with the Lord.

Through Christ's intercession we receive more than rescue from destruction.

We also receive the promise of everlasting happiness.

Notice how Moses pleaded.

We find grace in God's sight when we have received grace in our hearts that directs and strengthens us to do our duty.

Moses spoke as someone who dreaded the thought of going forward without God's presence.

God's gracious promises and past kindness should not merely strengthen our trust.

They should also make us more earnest in prayer.

And notice how Moses prevailed.

His intercession foreshadowed Christ's, which continues forever on behalf of all who come to God through him.

Christ's intercession does not depend on any merit in those for whom he prays.

Moses also asked to see God's glory, and even that request was heard.

A complete revelation of that glory would have overwhelmed Moses himself.

Human beings are too lowly and unworthy, too weak to bear it, and too guilty not to fear it.

Only God's merciful revelation of himself through Jesus Christ can be endured by us.

Yet the Lord granted Moses enough to satisfy him abundantly.

God's goodness is his glory.

He would have us know him more by the glory of his mercy than by the glory of his majesty.

The rock gave Moses a suitable place from which to see God's goodness and glory.

The rock at Horeb pointed to Christ, the Rock of refuge, salvation and strength.

Happy are those who stand upon this Rock!

The cleft in it may also picture Christ as struck, crucified, wounded and slain.

The account then reminds us that even our knowledge of God through Christ is incomplete in this life.

Compared with the sight of him that awaits us in heaven, it is like seeing only the back of someone who has passed by.

The clearest revelation of God's glory, grace and goodness in Christ is reserved for the life to come.
classic_reading:
[Exod.33.1-Exod.33.6]
Chapter 33
Chapter Outline
The Lord refuses to go with Israel. | (1-6) |
The tabernacle of Moses removed without the camp. | (7-11) |
Moses desires to see the glory of God. | (12-23) |
Verses 1-6
Those whom God pardons, must be made to know what their sin deserved. "Let them go forward as they are;" this was very expressive of God's displeasure. Though he promises to make good his covenant with Abraham, in giving them Canaan, yet he denies them the tokens of his presence they had been blessed with. The people mourned for their sin. Of all the bitter fruits and consequences of sin, true penitents most lament, and dread most, God's departure from them. Canaan itself would be no pleasant land without the Lord's presence. Those who parted with ornaments to maintain sin, could do no less than lay aside ornaments, in token of sorrow and shame for it.
[Exod.33.7-Exod.33.11]
Verses 7-11
Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp. This seems to have been a temporary building, set up for worship, and at which he judged disputes among the people. The people looked after him; they were very desirous to be at peace with God, and concerned to know what would come to pass. The cloudy pillar which had withdrawn from the camp when it was polluted with idolatry, now returned. If our hearts go forth toward God to meet him, he will graciously come to meet us.
[Exod.33.12-Exod.33.23]
Verses 12-23
Moses is very earnest with God. Thus, by the intercession of Christ, we are not only saved from ruin, but become entitled to everlasting happiness. Observe here how he pleads. We find grace in God's sight, if we find grace in our hearts to guide and quicken us in the way of our duty. Moses speaks as one who dreaded the thought of going forward without the Lord's presence. God's gracious promises, and mercy towards us, should not only encourage our faith, but also excite our fervency in prayer. Observe how he speeds. See, in a type, Christ's intercession, which he ever lives to make for all that come to God by him; and that it is not by any thing in those for whom he intercedes. Moses then entreats a sight of God's glory, and is heard in that also. A full discovery of the glory of God, would overwhelm even Moses himself. Man is mean, and unworthy of it; weak, and could not bear it; guilty, and could not but dread it. The merciful display which is made in Christ Jesus, alone can be borne by us. The Lord granted that which would abundantly satisfy. God's goodness is his glory; and he will have us to know him by the glory of his mercy, more than by the glory of his majesty. Upon the rock there was a fit place for Moses to view the goodness and glory of God. The rock in Horeb was typical of Christ the Rock; the Rock of refuge, salvation, and strength. Happy are they who stand upon this Rock. The cleft may be an emblem of Christ, as smitten, crucified, wounded, and slain. What follows, denotes the imperfect knowledge of God in the present state, even as revealed in Christ; for this, when compared with the heavenly sight of him. is but like seeing a man that is gone by, whose back only is to be seen. God in Christ, as he is, even the fullest and brightest displays of his glory, grace, and goodness, are reserved to another state.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe tables of the law renewed.1–4The name of the Lord proclaimed, The entreaty of Moses.5–9God's covenant.10–17The festivals.18–27The vail of Moses.28–35
God renews the stone tablets (verses 1–4)

When God created humanity in his own image, he wrote the moral law directly upon the human heart through his own power.

No outward instrument was needed.

But humanity broke the covenant.

Since then, the Lord has used human servants to write the law in Scripture and has also worked through them as he writes it anew upon people's hearts.

When he was reconciled to Israel, he ordered the stone tablets to be replaced and wrote his law on them.

Even under the gospel of peace through Christ, the moral law remains binding upon believers.

Christ has redeemed us from the law's curse, but not from its commands.

The earliest and surest sign that sin has been forgiven and peace made with God is that his law has been written upon the heart.

God proclaims his name and character (verses 5–9)

The Lord descended in a cloud, openly showing his presence and a glimpse of his glory.

He proclaimed his name—the divine qualities and character signified by Jehovah.

The Lord is merciful. He is ready to forgive sinners and help those in need.

He is gracious. He is kind and freely gives benefits that no one deserves.

He is patient. He is slow to anger, allowing time for repentance and punishing only when punishment is necessary.

He abounds in goodness and truth.

Even sinners receive his generous gifts, though they often misuse them.

Everything he reveals is unfailing truth, and everything he promises he faithfully performs.

He keeps mercy for thousands.

He continually shows kindness to sinners.

His store of mercy will never be exhausted, even to the end of time.

He forgives iniquity, transgression and sin.

His goodness includes the full and free forgiveness of wrongdoing.

Yet he will never treat the guilty as innocent.

God's holiness and justice are part of his goodness and love toward all his creatures.

In Christ's suffering, divine holiness and justice are displayed fully, and the true evil of sin is revealed.

God's forgiving mercy is always joined to grace that changes us and makes us holy.

None are pardoned without repentance and turning away from the deliberate practice of sin.

Those who abuse, neglect or despise this great salvation will not escape judgment.

Moses bowed before God and worshiped reverently.

Every aspect of God's revealed character gives believers reason to plead for forgiveness, holiness of heart and the growth of the Redeemer's kingdom.

Israel is warned against idolatry (verses 10–17)

The Israelites were ordered to destroy every object and monument connected with idolatry, however beautiful or expensive.

They were to refuse alliances, friendships and marriages that would draw them into the worship of false gods.

They were also to avoid idolatrous feasts.

God reminded them not to repeat their sin of making a metal image for worship.

Human jealousy is described as a fierce passion (Proverbs 6:34).

But God's jealousy is holy and righteous displeasure.

No one can worship God rightly without worshiping him alone.

The festivals and renewed covenant (verses 18–27)

Israel must rest one day every week.

Even plowing and harvesting had to stop.

Ordinary work must give way to holy rest, even when the harvest was ready.

Henry argues that observing the Sabbath during harvest would leave their work better blessed.

They were to show that they valued fellowship with God and their duty to him above the labor and joy of gathering crops.

Three times each year the people were to appear before the Lord God of Israel.

Canaan was a desirable land, and neighboring nations wanted its riches.

Yet God promised that those nations would not desire to seize Israel's land while the people gathered to worship.

Let us restrain sinful desires in our own hearts—especially anything that opposes God's glory.

Then let us trust him to restrain the evil desires of others against us.

The way of duty is the way of safety.

Those who risk things for God's sake never finally lose through serving him.

Three feasts are named.

First, Passover remembered the deliverance from Egypt.

Second, the Feast of Weeks, or Pentecost, included the offering of firstfruits.

Third, the Feast of Ingathering, or Tabernacles, marked the gathering of the harvest.

Moses was commanded to write God's words so the people would know and understand them better.

We can never be thankful enough for the written word of God.

The Lord made his covenant with Israel through Moses as mediator.

In the same way, the covenant of grace is made with believers through Christ.

Moses' shining face and the veil (verses 28–35)

Deep spiritual fellowship with God strengthens and beautifies a renewed, holy character.

Sincere godliness can give a person's face a brightness that wins respect and love.

The veil Moses wore showed how much less clearly God's revelation was understood under the old covenant than it would be under the gospel.

It also pictured the natural veil over human hearts that prevents people from understanding spiritual realities.

Henry further applies the image to Israel's continuing difficulty in recognizing Christ.

He says this veil can be removed only through the Lord's Spirit, who reveals Christ as the goal of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

Fear and unbelief can also place a veil before us, hindering our free approach to the mercy seat above.

We should tell our heavenly Father about all our needs, both earthly and spiritual.

Let us speak openly of our obstacles, struggles, trials and temptations.

Let us confess our sins.

[Exod.34.1-Exod.34.4]
Chapter 34
Chapter Outline
The tables of the law renewed. | (1-4) |
The name of the Lord proclaimed, The entreaty of Moses. | (5-9) |
God's covenant. | (10-17) |
The festivals. | (18-27) |
The vail of Moses. | (28-35) |
Verses 1-4
When God made man in his own image, the moral law was written in his heart, by the finger of God, without outward means. But since the covenant then made with man was broken, the Lord has used the ministry of men, both in writing the law in the Scriptures, and in writing it in the heart. When God was reconciled to the Israelites, he ordered the tables to be renewed, and wrote his law in them. Even under the gospel of peace by Christ, the moral law continues to bind believers. Though Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, yet not from the commands of it. The first and the best evidence of the pardon of sin, and peace with God, is the writing the law in the heart.
[Exod.34.5-Exod.34.9]
Verses 5-9
The Lord descended by some open token of his presence and manifestation of his glory in a cloud, and thence proclaimed his NAME; that is, the perfections and character which are denoted by the name JEHOVAH. The Lord God is merciful; ready to forgive the sinner, and to relieve the needy. Gracious; kind, and ready to bestow undeserved benefits. Long-suffering; slow to anger, giving time for repentance, only punishing when it is needful. He is abundant in goodness and truth; even sinners receive the riches of his bounty abundantly, though they abuse them. All he reveals is infallible truth, all he promises is in faithfulness. Keeping mercy for thousands; he continually shows mercy to sinners, and has treasures, which cannot be exhausted, to the end of time. Forgiving iniquity, and transgression, and sin; his mercy and goodness reach to the full and free forgiveness of sin. And will by no means clear the guilty; the holiness and justice of God are part of his goodness and love towards all his creatures. In Christ's sufferings, the Divine holiness and justice are fully shown, and the evil of sin is made known. God's forgiving mercy is always attended by his converting, sanctifying grace. None are pardoned but those who repent and forsake the allowed practice of every sin; nor shall any escape, who abuse, neglect, or despise this great salvation. Moses bowed down, and worshipped reverently. Every perfection in the name of God, the believer may plead with Him for the forgiveness of his sins, the making holy of his heart, and the enlargement of the Redeemer's kingdom.
[Exod.34.10-Exod.34.17]
Verses 10-17
The Israelites are commanded to destroy every monument of idolatry, however curious or costly; to refuse all alliance, friendship, or marriage with idolaters, and all idolatrous feasts; and they were reminded not with idolaters, and all idolatrous feats; and they were reminded not to repeat the crime of making molten images. Jealously is called the rage of a man, [Prov.6.34] Pr 6:34; but in God it is holy and just displeasure. Those cannot worship God aright, who do not worship him only.
[Exod.34.18-Exod.34.27]
Verses 18-27
Once a week they must rest, even in ploughing time, and in harvest. All worldly business must give way to that holy rest; even harvest work will prosper the better, for the religious observance of the sabbath day in harvest time. We must show that we prefer our communion with God, and our duty to him, before the business or the joy of harvest. Thrice a year they must appear before the Lord God, the God of Israel. Canaan was a desirable land, and the neighbouring nations were greedy; yet God says, They shall not desire it. Moses is to write these words, that the people might know them better. We can never be enough thankful to God for the written word. God would make a covenant with Israel, in Moses as a mediator. The Sabbath is to be kept (verses 1–3)

Christ's yoke is gentle and easy.

Because of him, our Sabbath duties are more joyful and its restrictions less burdensome than they were for the Jews under the old covenant.

But that only makes us more guilty if we neglect them.

God wisely gave us a Sabbath for merciful purposes.

It is sinful to treat this gift with contempt.

How can we despise a blessed day that the generous Lord has given us to grow in grace with the church on earth and prepare for happiness with the church in heaven?

Freely given materials and skilled work (verses 4–19)

The tabernacle would be dedicated to God's honor and used in his service.

Therefore, every contribution toward it was an offering to the Lord.

The rule was simple: whoever had a willing heart should bring a gift.

Everyone with the necessary skill was to do the work.

God distributes different gifts among his people.

Each person should use the gift received in service to others (1 Peter 4:10).

Those with wealth were to provide materials.

Those with skill were to use their abilities for the sanctuary.

The two groups needed each other, and the tabernacle needed them both (1 Corinthians 12:7–21).

The people give willingly (verses 20–29)

Without willing hearts, even very expensive offerings would be hateful to God.

But with genuine willingness, even the smallest gift is accepted.

We show that our hearts are willing when we gladly help the work of God advance.

People who work diligently and contentedly in humble occupations are just as acceptable to God as those who perform impressive public service.

The women who spun goats' hair were called wise-hearted, because they did the work wholeheartedly for the Lord.

Likewise, a laborer, craftsperson or servant who carries out ordinary work in faith and reverence for God may show as much wisdom in that calling as a highly useful minister.

Both are accepted by the same Lord.

Our wisdom and duty lie in giving God the glory for our abilities and using them for his purposes, whether we have many talents or few.

Bezalel and Oholiab lead and teach the work (verses 30–35)

God himself appointed the master craftsmen.

This prevented disputes over who should lead the work.

It also ensured that everyone who took part knew whose instructions to follow and to whom they were accountable.

God filled those whom he called by name with his Spirit.

Skill—even skill used in ordinary trades—is God's gift from above.

Yet some people are very good at assigning tasks to others.

They can explain exactly what everyone else should do, but refuse to lift a finger themselves.

Such people behave like lazy servants.

Bezalel and Oholiab were to do more than invent plans.

They had to carry out the work themselves and teach others to do it.

Those who lead should teach.

And anyone to whom God has given knowledge should gladly share it for the benefit of other people.

The builders' faithfulness and the tabernacle's meaning

The builders began their work with eagerness and zeal.

They followed their instructions exactly.

And they were faithful enough to object when people brought more contributions than were needed.

Their example deserves to be followed.

We should serve God with that same readiness, care and honesty.

We should also serve those in authority over us faithfully in everything that is lawful.

Everyone entrusted with public responsibilities should hate dishonest gain and avoid every opportunity or temptation to become greedy.

Where do we see God's love toward us pictured so clearly—the love by which we live in him and he lives in us?

We see it in Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23).

This is the heart of the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

It was also the purpose of the tabernacle of testimony.

The sanctuary visibly declared God's love for the human race, despite the fall from humanity's original condition.

That love was displayed fully when Christ came to live on earth.

The Word became flesh (John 1:14).

As the original expression suggests, he pitched his tabernacle among us.

Original heading

The making of the ark, and the furniture of the tabernacle.

The furnishings as pictures of worship and redemption

The furniture of the tabernacle pointed toward the spiritual worship that God accepts.

The incense represented the prayers of the saints.

The sacrifice offered on the altar pointed to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

The golden jar of manna, the bread from heaven, pointed to the flesh of Jesus Christ, which he gave for the life of the world.

The lampstand, with its burning lights, represented the teaching and illumination of the Holy Spirit.

The bread of the Presence pictured the abundant provision God gives to people who hunger and thirst for righteousness.

That provision is supplied through the gospel, the appointed means of grace and the sacraments celebrated in God's house of prayer.

The craftsmen took great care to follow the rule God gave them.

We should imitate that obedience.

Let us seek the Holy Spirit's influence, so that we may rejoice in God and glorify him during our earthly lives.

And in the end, may we dwell with him forever.

--In the furniture of the tabernacle were emblems of a spiritual and acceptable service. The incense represented the prayers of the saints. The sacrifice of the alter represented the Lamb of God that taketh away the sins of the world. The golden pot with manna, or bread from heaven, the flesh of Jesus Christ, which he gave for the life of the world. The candlestick, with its lights, the teaching and enlightening of the Holy Spirit. The shew-bread represented that provision for those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, which the gospel, the ordinances and the sacraments of the house of prayer, abundantly bestow. The exactness of the workmen to their rule, should be followed by us; seeking for the influences of the Holy Spirit, that we may rejoice in and glorify God while in this world, and at length be with him for ever.

The bronze altar and basin (verses 1–8)

In every age of the church, some people have been especially devoted to God.

They attend faithfully to his appointed worship and are more willing than others to surrender even things they have a perfect right to keep for his sake.

Some women of Israel were deeply committed to the Lord and zealous for worship in the tabernacle.

They showed that zeal by giving up their mirrors.

These were polished bronze plates, which served the purpose of looking glasses before glass mirrors had been invented.

The women chose to give up something valuable and useful so that it could serve the Lord.

The court and its curtains (verses 9–20)

The walls around the tabernacle's court were only curtains.

Henry understands this as a reminder that the Jewish church's outward form was temporary and could change.

In time, that arrangement would be taken down and folded away.

The space occupied by the tent would then be enlarged, and its ropes extended, so that the Gentile world could be welcomed in.

The offerings and the meaning of the sanctuary (verses 21–31)

The foundation was made from heavy pieces of silver.

They pointed to the strength and purity of the truth upon which the church is founded.

As we read about the tabernacle's furnishings, let us keep our eyes on the Lord Jesus Christ.

When we look at the altar for burnt offerings, let us see Jesus.

In his righteousness and salvation there is a full and sufficient offering for sin.

Let our souls be washed in the basin of regeneration by his Holy Spirit, so that we may be clean.

And just as the Israelites gave willingly, may our own hearts be made willing.

Let us be ready to surrender anything for Christ and count everything else as loss in order to gain him.

The priestly garments are completed (verses 1–31)

The priests' clothing was rich and beautiful.

In the early life of the church, these visible symbols taught people about greater blessings that would come later.

But the reality to which they pointed is Christ and the grace of his gospel.

Christ is our great High Priest.

When he undertook to redeem us, he clothed himself for service.

He received and displayed the gifts and graces of the Spirit.

He fastened himself to his purpose, resolved to complete the task.

He took responsibility for all God's spiritual Israel.

He kept his people close to his heart, engraved them on the palms of his hands and presented them before his Father.

He crowned himself with holiness to the Lord, dedicating all his saving work to the honor of his Father's holiness.

True believers are also spiritual priests.

The pure linen of their clothing for service represents the righteousness of the saints (Revelation 19:8).

The tabernacle is completed (verses 32–43)

The tabernacle was a picture of Jesus Christ.

The Most High was visibly present in the sanctuary above the ark.

In the same way, God dwelt in the human nature of his beloved Son.

In Christ, all the fullness of deity lives bodily (Colossians 2:9).

The tabernacle also pictured every genuine Christian.

God the Father dwells in the soul of each true follower of the Savior.

He is the One that person worships and the source of every blessing enjoyed.

The tabernacle also represented the Redeemer's church.

The poorest and the most powerful are equally dear to the Father's love, freely given through faith in Christ.

Finally, the tabernacle was a picture of the heavenly temple (Revelation 21:3).

How magnificent will God's glory appear when the cloud is removed and his faithful worshipers see him as he truly is!

The tabernacle is to be raised and the priests consecrated (verses 1–15)

Whenever a new year begins, we should seek to serve God better than we did in the previous year.

The tabernacle was completed in only half a year.

When many people are deeply committed to a good cause, much can be accomplished in a short time.

And when God's commands are continually followed as the rule for the work, everything will be done well.

The high priesthood remained within Aaron's family until Christ came.

In him—the reality to which all these earlier shadows pointed—the priesthood continues forever.

Moses carries out everything God commanded (verses 16–33)

When the tabernacle and its furnishings were ready, Israel did not postpone erecting it until the people reached Canaan.

They obeyed God's will and set it up in the middle of their camp.

People whose lives are unsettled must never use their circumstances as an excuse to neglect worship and faith.

We cannot say that it is enough to begin serving God after our lives have become stable.

No.

We need a tabernacle for God even in the wilderness.

Indeed, we may enter the next world before we ever find a settled home in this one.

We must also be careful not to deceive ourselves with an outward appearance of godliness.

The fact that so few of those who left Egypt eventually entered Canaan should warn young people in particular against putting off the care of their souls.

God's glory fills and guides the tabernacle (verses 34–38)

A cloud covered the tabernacle even on the clearest days.

It was not an ordinary cloud that sunlight could scatter.

All Israel could see it day and night as a sign of God's presence.

They should never again need to ask whether the Lord was truly among them.

The cloud guided the entire camp through the wilderness.

When it rested over the sanctuary, the people stayed where they were.

When it moved, they followed.

The Lord's glory filled the tabernacle.

In light and fire, the Shekinah—the visible sign of God's presence—made itself known.

God is light.

Our God is also a consuming fire.

The light was so dazzling and the fire so fearsome that Moses could not enter the tent of meeting until its splendor diminished.

But what Moses could not do, our Lord Jesus has accomplished.

God caused him to draw near.

And Jesus now invites us to come boldly even to the mercy seat.

The Holy Spirit teaches us to follow Christ's example as well as depend upon him.

If we attend to his appointed worship and obey his commands, we will not lose our way.

He will guide us along right paths until we reach heaven, where his holiness dwells.

Blessed be God for Jesus Christ!
